note: The running update log shown at /ps/updates, newest first. Add an entry in the SAME commit as the change it describes, so it arrives reviewable in the diff rather than being reconstructed later from git log. Keep it partner-and-team readable: what changed and why it matters, not the file names.

updates.title: Adoption by feature — a second slice of Org Features
updates.body: The report has always answered "how much of the platform does this organization use". It now also answers "how far has this feature spread", which is the same data transposed and a genuinely different question. Two tabs at the top switch between them.
items: One row per feature: its share of the organizations live on rec.us, a letter grade, a trend sparkline and the signed change since the first comparable measurement. Sortable on every column, and a row opens the organizations behind it.

Pre-launch organizations are out of the denominator. Half the fleet is mid-setup and has configured almost nothing, so counting them makes every feature look unpopular — the all-organization figure is still on every row beside it.

The grade comes off its own scale. An organization using 25% of the platform and a feature reaching 25% of the fleet are not comparable facts, so the feature ramp is a separate measurement — currently A 14 · B 8 · C 11 · D 11 · F 13 across the 57 tracked features.

The trend works from today rather than in two days: the per-feature series was backfilled from the daily snapshots this project has already committed. Seb is up 4 points since 7 September, store credit and desk locations 2, SMS 2.

25 older snapshots were deliberately left out of the series. They predate the launch flag, so their live-organization count is zero and there is no share to take from them — plotting one anyway would publish a change in who we measure as a change in adoption.

updates.title: Filter Org Features to one feature — and calendar sync is now tracked
updates.body: Two halves of the same gap: the catalog had no entry for calendar sync, and there was no way to ask "who uses X" for anything outside the eight features with a chip.
items: A feature picker beside the organization pulldown lists every tracked feature, grouped by category, with the number of organizations using it printed on each option — so the count is readable without picking anything.
Every feature now has its own page: how many organizations use it, how many of those are live on rec.us, and — the list that is actually actionable — who does not, split live from pre-launch.

Calendar sync joins the catalog as the 58th feature. 20 organizations have ever connected a Google or Outlook calendar, 18 are connected today, and 62 calendars are synced between them. City of Bloomington leads on 11.

Two organizations have a badly broken connection worth chasing: Hermosa Beach has 1,098 failed syncs against 1 success, and Euclid 887 of 1,761. A further 13 calendar views across 12 organizations have been switched off automatically after the sign-in to Google or Outlook stopped working.

Adoption is now scored over 57 features instead of 56, so every score moves by about a point and the trend sparkline is blank until the daily bake has two readings on the new set. A score taken over a different set of features is a different measurement, so the old points are dropped rather than plotted.

updates.title: Org Features has settings — choose which features count, and exclude organizations
updates.body: The gear on the Feature usage panel opens a shared settings sheet. It scopes the page; it never deletes anything.
items: Untick a feature and it leaves the adoption score's denominator, the per-organization checklist and the A/B gap list. "How adopted is this org" only means something against the features you care about.
Tick an organization to drop it from the page entirely — the table, the pulldown, both comparison slots, the fleet average and the count. For test and retired accounts.
The settings are SHARED by everyone on the CX dashboard, so Save is a deliberate action rather than an auto-save, and the page records who last changed them.

Whatever the settings scope out is stated on screen above the table, with a note that the scores are not comparable with a differently-scoped view. A count that quietly drops organizations is how a fleet figure stops being trusted.
Nothing ticked reads as "not measured", never as 0% — an empty denominator is not an organization that adopted nothing.

updates.title: All 56 measurable features are now measured, and the org list includes accounts that have not launched
updates.body: The dashboard measured 18 of 57 catalogued features. It now measures 56 — everything the database can actually answer.
items: 56 of 57 features measured, up from 18. The 39 that read 'Not yet measured' now carry real numbers.

Sandbox organizations are gone (23 of them), and organizations that have not launched yet are now included and marked. 144 organizations: 73 live on rec.us, 71 not. An org mid-configuration is exactly who an adoption dashboard is for, so they are shown rather than hidden — but they are flagged, and they are not averaged into a fleet figure unlabelled.
Account Health opens sorted alphabetically. It opened on open-bug count, which buried whichever account you came to look at.

The widest-adopted features across launched orgs: facility rentals 72 of 73, member booking windows 71, policies and waivers 70, seasons 66, email 65, skill levels 64. The thinnest: physical access devices 1, guest participation 5, custom sending domains 8, gift cards 8, structured refund policies 8.
Fleet adoption now reads about a third rather than half. That is the denominator tripling from 18 features to 56, not organizations going backwards.

Six of the catalogued measurement definitions turned out to be wrong and were corrected against the live database, including one that would have reported every organization as using a feature that does not exist in the schema at all.
One feature stays unmeasured on purpose — Invite-Only / Restricted Registration. There is no field for it; the page says so rather than showing a made-up number.

updates.title: Now measuring events, ticket sales and Seb — and the snapshot was 16 days old
updates.body: Dan: "there's a bunch of stuff we're NOT measuring here. Events/ticket sales, SMS usage, Seb usage." Two of the three were missing entirely; SMS was already there.
items: Four new measurements: Events, Event Ticket Sales, Seb (AI Assistant) and Seb Routines. The dashboard now measures 18 of 57 catalogued features, up from 14.
Seb is the widest adoption of the four: 43 of 73 organizations have asked it something, 2,367 questions in total. Apex 484, El Segundo 316, Torrance 263, Hermosa Beach 230, Douglas County 227.
Ticket sales: 11,470 tickets sold across 15 organizations. Jurupa leads with 6,267, then Torrance 4,210 and Chico 601. Events themselves: 124 across 24 organizations.
Seb Routines — scheduled jobs an org has set up — are still early: 33 across 10 organizations, led by Hermosa Beach with 9.
SMS was already measured and is unchanged: 17 organizations, 17,167 messages sent, led by West Haven with 5,244.
The fleet adoption figure moved from 56% to 51%. That is the denominator growing from 14 measured features to 18, not orgs going backwards — which is why the card states the denominator out loud.
The snapshot itself was also 16 days stale (the daily refresh had not run since 22 August) and is now current, with 73 published organizations, up from 69.

updates.title: Org Features: the pills are back, alphabetical order, and you can compare two orgs
updates.body: Four fixes to the Org Features section, all from Dan looking at it.
items: The metric columns are heat-coloured pills again, the way the standalone dashboard shows them. The colour scale is now shared between the two pages rather than written twice, so the same number cannot read as a different colour depending which page you opened.
Organizations are listed alphabetically. They were sorted by adoption score, which means you had to already know an org's score to find it in a list of 69.
The filter is a pulldown of every organization instead of a search box. The list is known and closed, so a typo in a text box could only ever empty the table.

You can compare two organizations: pick A and B and they render as two rows over the same columns, with a line naming the features each one has that the other does not. It stays hidden until both slots are filled — a one-row comparison is not one.
Fleet adoption no longer moves when you filter to a single org. It is a fleet figure, so it is computed over all of them.
The public dashboard's link still said 'PS Dashboard' after the rename. Fixed — half a rename is worse than none.

updates.title: The bug list was five weeks stale — refreshed, plus a filter by org
updates.body: Dan spotted that every status on Bug Management was out of date. It was: the bug half of this dashboard's snapshot was built once on 31 July and nothing had rebuilt it since.
items: The bug list is current again. It moved from 241 open bugs to 285 — and six of the seven rows at the top of the Urgent list had already been closed. Urgent read 7; the real number is 2. PLA-1880, the row at the very top, went Done on 4 August.
You can now filter the list by org. Options are the Linear customers attached to open bugs, busiest first, with a count beside each.

The filter says what it hides. Only 44 of the 285 open bugs are tagged to any org, so picking one shows what is tagged to that org and not everything that affects it — the note under the filter spells that out rather than letting a small number read as a total.

Org names are shown exactly as Linear holds them, and are deliberately not merged. Linear has separate customer records for some orgs (Chico and City of Chico, Smyrna and Smyrnaga, three spellings of Jurupa Valley including a typo), so a couple of orgs appear twice. Guessing which records are the same org would sometimes merge two different ones, silently. Giving each Linear customer the Rec org ID as its external ID is what would fix it properly.

The sidebar now says how old the snapshot is, and turns amber past two days. It used to say 'refreshed daily' — which it kept saying for 38 days while nothing refreshed it. That claim is why nobody noticed.

The rebuild is a script now rather than something done by hand, and it refuses to write a snapshot that still contains closed bugs. Putting it on a daily schedule needs the Linear connector attached to a Routine, which has to be done from the Routines screen.

updates.title: The Rec logo, a rename, and Org Features stops throwing you out of the dashboard
updates.body: Navigation cleanup, plus two new sections under Admin.
items: The Rec mark is now in the top-left corner. It is the same asset the reporting project uses rather than a redrawn one, so the two internal surfaces look like the same product.
'PS dashboard' is now 'CX dashboard'. The label only — every /ps/... link anyone has bookmarked still works, and the data behind it is untouched.

Org Features is now a section INSIDE this dashboard. It used to be a plain link that navigated out of the app entirely, so the sidebar vanished and there was no way back. It reads the same public snapshot the standalone dashboard does, so the two cannot disagree about an adoption score, and clicking an organization expands its feature checklist in place rather than navigating away.
This page, and the 'How This Works' page describing how the project is put together.
The fleet adoption average is taken over the organizations we could actually score, not over all of them — an org the bake has not measured is not folded in as a zero.

updates.title: Postgres behind the scenes, and CI that actually runs
updates.body: Two structural changes. Neither changes a number on any page.
items: User accounts now live in Postgres instead of on the server's attached disk. They are the only thing this app writes at runtime and the only thing it cannot rebuild — every snapshot can be re-baked, but a password nobody has a copy of is gone.

That is what lets the disk be detached later, which is what lets the service update without going offline for a minute each time. The reporting project made the same change yesterday and its deploys are now invisible to anyone using it.
It ships switched off: with no database configured the app behaves exactly as it did before, which the automated boot check proves on every commit.
CI now runs on every change: the code parses, the pages' inline React parses, the tests run, and the committed data snapshots are checked for valid JSON with the keys the pages read.

That last check matters most — the daily refresh commits a new snapshot straight to the live branch, so a broken bake used to be able to take the dashboard down with no code change. Now it fails the check instead of deploying.

updates.title: The daily refresh is running again
updates.body: The scheduled job that re-bakes the feature snapshot each morning had been paused since 23 August, so the dashboard had been serving 16-day-old numbers while claiming to refresh daily.
items: Re-enabled and verified with a run rather than left to prove itself at 6am.
Worth knowing for next time: the dashboard gives no sign that its data is stale. The snapshot date is in the sidebar footer, and that is the only place it shows.
